intro:
These exercises do not ask you to invent cryptography. They ask you to give a proof system the systems shape it needs to be operable: a public statement, a private witness that never crosses the verification boundary, and a proof artifact that travels like versioned transport data. Each exercise targets one place where ordinary backend intuition quietly leads you wrong, and turns it into a concrete Rust type or service boundary.

The thread running through all of them is the single handoff the chapter keeps returning to: everything up to and including the prover holds the secret witness, and from the proof artifact onward only public data crosses. Get that boundary into the type system and most of the integration failures, leaks, over-retention, and prover/verifier disagreements stop being possible by construction. The lab makes that boundary executable.

exerciseSolutions.title: Separate public inputs, private witnesses, and proofs
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Take the billing flow apart by asking the chapter's framing question of every field: what is the verifier supposed to learn by design? The public credit limit and the public committed digest are public inputs. They are part of the statement the verifier checks against, they can be logged at the verification boundary, and they can be routed more broadly without breaking the privacy goal. The private line items are witness-only. They are exactly the data the proof exists to keep hidden, so they must never cross the verification boundary, never appear in a verifier-facing DTO, and never land in a log line read by a system that only needs to verify.

The proof is a third, distinct artifact. It is not the witness in disguise and it is not a hashed copy of the line items; it is the cryptographic evidence that a valid witness exists for this statement. The mistake the exercise is guarding against is treating the proof as if it were the witness, for instance by stashing line items 'inside' the proof record or by assuming the proof must be as sensitive as the secrets it was built from. The proving key and verification key are a fourth and fifth class of object: the proving key is a setup artifact the prover needs, the verification key is a setup artifact the verifier needs, and neither is the proof itself.

The logging and transport consequence falls straight out of the classification. The public total, public limit, and public commitment are safe to log at the verifier boundary; they are what the verifier is designed to see. The line items are not safe to log there, and they should not be present at that boundary at all. If the verifier ever sees the raw line items, the system might still compute the right answer, but it is no longer zero-knowledge in the intended sense, because the secret the proof was supposed to protect has been disclosed through a side channel rather than through the proof.
criteria: Public credit limit and committed digest are named as statement data; line items are named as witness data, keeping the two classes distinct.
The proof is identified as its own artifact, separate from the witness, and the proving/verification keys are called out as setup artifacts rather than the proof.
Logging consequence is stated: public fields are safe at the verifier boundary, line items are not, and leaking them defeats zero-knowledge even if the result is still correct.

exerciseSolutions.title: Refactor an API workflow so proving and verification are isolated
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The handler conflates two service shapes that the chapter insists on separating. Witness derivation and proof generation are heavy, secret-handling work; they belong in a proving worker or background lane, not on the request thread. Verifying the proof again locally inside the same handler is redundant: the point of a proof is that any holder of the statement and the proof can check it cheaply, so re-verifying inline on the proving path adds latency without adding trust. Move witness derivation and proof generation off the request handler into an asynchronous proving lane, and let the request edge enqueue work and return a handle.

The boundary that should receive only the statement plus the proof artifact is the verifier. The verifier never needs the witness, so the verification request type must not carry witness fields at all. The custody mistake in the original workflow is storing the proof and the witness together in one outbound record. That is how private witness data leaks or gets over-retained: the witness rides along into storage, backups, and downstream consumers that only ever needed to verify, and now every copy of that record is a place the secret can escape. The repair is to split storage so the witness stays proving-side with a short, deliberate retention window, while the statement and proof travel onward as their own artifact.

For the signal that inline proving is already hurting the edge, watch request-handler latency and its tail percentiles, plus the depth and age of any proving queue once the heavy work is moved off-thread. Inline proving shows up as a latency cliff on the API edge under load, because each request now pays full proving cost on the request thread. After the refactor, the design should expose proving-queue age and the verification failure rate as first-class metrics, so operators can see the heavy lane backing up before it becomes an outage and can distinguish a slow prover from a verifier that is rejecting proofs.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Heavy witness/proof work moves to a worker; the verifier-facing record carries statement plus proof only, never the witness.
criteria: Witness derivation and proof generation are moved out of the request handler into a proving worker, removing heavy work from the request thread.
Verifier input is separated from witness input: the verifiable record carries statement plus proof, and the verification path needs no witness fields.
The privacy/retention defect is named: storing proof and witness in one outbound record over-retains and risks leaking the secret.
Latency/queue signals are identified: request-handler tail latency before, proving-queue age and verification failure rate after.

exerciseSolutions.title: Define typed proving and verification requests
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The design goal is to make the boundary honest in the type system: witness material can only exist on the proving side, and the verification side is structurally incapable of carrying it. That means three distinct types rather than one struct that does every job. The ProofRequest owns the witness and the statement, because proving is the only operation that legitimately needs both. The VerificationRequest owns the statement and the proof artifact and nothing else, so an engineer literally cannot put a witness field where the verifier reads. The ProofArtifact is the produced evidence plus the public statement it commits to.

Every one of these types carries a circuit identity and protocol version explicitly, because the prover and verifier must agree on which circuit and which transcript rules are in force. Versioning artifacts and requests early is cheap; retrofitting it after the first migration costs a coordinated redeploy across every team that touches the boundary. The public statement fields (total and limit) live in one place, the Statement struct, which both the proving and verification sides embed. Keeping a single home for statement fields means the prover and verifier cannot drift on what the public inputs even are.

The tradeoff is a small amount of duplication: the statement is embedded in both requests, and the circuit identity appears on both the request and the artifact. That redundancy is deliberate. It buys a verification path that can be reviewed in isolation, with no path by which a witness field reaches it, and it keeps the whole design small enough that a reviewer can confirm the boundary at a glance rather than tracing control flow.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Witness lives only on ProofRequest; VerificationRequest carries statement plus artifact, and CircuitId pins circuit identity on both requests and the artifact.
criteria: ProofRequest and VerificationRequest are distinct structs with different fields, so the proving and verification boundaries are separated.
VerificationRequest contains no witness field, so the verification path cannot require witness-only data.
CircuitId (name plus version) is present on requests and on the artifact, giving an explicit circuit-identity and version field.
The type set is small and the witness lives in exactly one place, so another engineer can confirm the boundary quickly.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair transcript and serialization bugs before proofs go cross-service
exerciseSolutions.solution:
There are two independent defects, and both are protocol-compatibility bugs rather than ordinary runtime bugs. The first is the service that serializes public inputs through a map with unstable key order. A prover and verifier that hash the same fields in a different order are hashing different byte strings, so they derive different transcript challenges and verification fails intermittently, depending on whichever iteration order the map happened to produce in that deployment. The fix is canonical serialization: define a fixed field layout for the public inputs and serialize them in a deterministic order (an explicit field sequence, or a sorted-key encoding), so the same statement always produces the same bytes regardless of process, platform, or library version.

The second defect is the changed transcript domain string. The domain string is part of the transcript contract that prover and verifier share; it seeds the transcript and therefore feeds into every challenge derived from it. Changing it during a refactor is not a cosmetic rename, it is a protocol break: a prover on the new domain string and a verifier on the old one are operating in different challenge spaces and will never agree, exactly as the chapter's domain-separation example shows two different domains landing on different challenges by design. Restore the original domain string for the existing protocol version, and if a new domain is genuinely wanted, bump the protocol version alongside it so the change is explicit and gated.

These are protocol-compatibility bugs because each component is internally correct: the serializer serializes, the hasher hashes, the verifier verifies. The incompatibility only exists across the prover/verifier boundary, which is why local tests pass and cross-deployment verification fails. The drift-prevention check is a contract test in CI that pins both the canonical encoding and the domain string: hash a fixed set of public inputs and assert the bytes and the resulting challenge equal a committed golden value, so any future change to field order or domain string fails the build before rollout. The protocol or circuit version should be carried explicitly on the proof artifact (and the request), so a version mismatch is detected and rejected loudly instead of surfacing as a flaky verification failure.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Canonical sorted-key encoding fixes unstable map order; the domain string is pinned to a protocol version, and a contract test guards both.
criteria: Both repairs are named: canonical/deterministic serialization for the unstable map order, and restoring/version-gating the transcript domain string.
The defects are explained as protocol-compatibility bugs: components are locally correct but disagree across the prover/verifier boundary.
A CI/contract test is proposed that pins canonical bytes and the domain string against golden values, and the protocol version is carried on the artifact.

exerciseSolutions.title: Threat-model a proof-backed API or game mechanic
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Take a game mechanic where clients submit proofs to unlock rewards by proving a hidden state transition is valid (for example, proving a move was legal and a hidden resource total stayed within bounds without revealing the player's full hidden state). Separate the cryptographic assumptions from the Rust implementation and deployment assumptions throughout, because the failures cluster differently in each.

Privacy risk: the proof keeps the witness (the player's hidden state) secret, but metadata can still leak. The size of the proof, the timing of submissions, the choice of circuit, and the public inputs themselves can reveal which transition occurred or narrow the hidden state. A public input that is too revealing defeats the point even when the cryptography is sound, so the threat model must list what is public and confirm that the public statement alone does not disclose what the proof was meant to hide. Integrity risk: a forged or malformed proof that the verifier wrongly accepts, or a valid proof for a circuit that does not actually enforce the rules the designers think it does. This is the chapter's second illusion, that a passing verification implies a correct circuit; the model must call out circuit correctness as a trust assumption, not an established fact. Denial-of-service risk: the cheapest attack is usually resource exhaustion at the verifier, via giant proof artifacts that blow memory or parsing budgets, or a flood of invalid proofs that each cost a full verification before rejection. If the server also generates witnesses or proofs on demand, an attacker can request expensive proving work to exhaust the proving lane.

For the explicit trust assumption, call out the setup artifacts and key distribution: if the proving system uses a trusted setup, the soundness of every proof depends on that ceremony, and if the verification key is distributed or updated incorrectly, the verifier may accept proofs for the wrong circuit. Keep that cryptographic assumption clearly separate from the Rust and deployment assumptions, such as 'our serialization is canonical' and 'our verifier enforces a size limit before parsing.' For observability, expose at least the verification failure rate (a spike signals an attack or a deployment mismatch), inbound artifact size distribution (to catch oversized-artifact DoS), and proving-queue age (to catch expensive-witness exhaustion). Bound every input: cap artifact size before parsing, rate-limit submissions per client, and reject unknown circuit or protocol versions outright.
criteria: At least one privacy risk (metadata/public-input leakage), one integrity risk (forged proof or incorrect circuit), and one DoS risk (giant artifacts, invalid-proof floods, or expensive witness requests) are described.
Cryptographic assumptions (trusted setup, circuit correctness, key distribution) are kept explicitly separate from Rust/deployment assumptions (canonical serialization, size limits).
At least two observability hooks are named, such as verification failure rate, inbound artifact size, and proving-queue age.

exerciseSolutions.title: Plan witness generation, artifact custody, and hardware lanes for a proof workflow
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Draw the pipeline as distinct stages with explicit handoffs. Circuit or model compilation ends when you have a compiled circuit (and its derived proving key and verification key) that is fixed for a given circuit version; it is a build-time artifact, content-addressed by a circuit ID, and it does not change per request. Witness generation begins per request: it takes the private inputs plus the public statement and produces a witness that satisfies the compiled circuit. The two are separate stages because they have different lifetimes and different custody rules. Compiled circuits and keys are long-lived, shared, and cacheable; witnesses are short-lived, secret, and per-request, and they must not be persisted alongside proofs.

The artifacts to make explicit, and their custody rules: the circuit ID (content-addressed, the anchor everything else hangs off), the proving key (large, versioned with the circuit, lives on the proving lane), the verification key (small, versioned with the circuit, distributed to the verifier lane), the witness schema (versioned, so prover and verifier agree on input layout), and the proof blob (versioned transport data, carries the circuit ID). The custody rule is that the proving key and verification key are content-addressed and pinned to the circuit ID, so a verifier can never accidentally check a proof against the wrong circuit, and the witness is never cached or content-addressed because it is secret and must be dropped after proving.

GPU acceleration, if any, belongs in the proving stage (witness generation and proof generation are the heavy compute), never at the verifier, which is meant to be small and cheap. Isolate that boundary the way the chapter isolates heavy accelerator lanes: the proving lane runs on its own GPU-backed workers behind a queue, with its own scaling and failure modes, while the API edge and the verifier stay lightweight and CPU-only. The rollout gate before several teams depend on the verifier output: pin the circuit ID, proving key, and verification key versions together and require a contract test (a known statement plus witness produces a proof the current verification key accepts) to pass in CI before any mixed deployment, so a verifier on one circuit version can never be paired with proofs from another. Make artifact ownership boring and content-addressed enough that operations and incident response can answer 'which circuit produced this proof' from the artifact alone.
criteria: Compiled circuit/model artifacts (and keys) are distinguished from per-request witness generation and from the proof artifact, with their differing lifetimes stated.
At least three explicit artifacts are named (circuit ID, proving key, verification key, witness schema, proof blob) plus a versioning/custody rule (content-addressing pinned to circuit ID).
GPU acceleration is placed in the proving lane and isolated behind a queue, keeping the verifier lane lightweight and separate from the API edge.
A rollout/testing gate is given: pinned key versions plus a contract test that a fresh proof is accepted, required before mixed deployments.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
verified = true
public total = 45
proof bytes = 96
labSolution.explanation:
The lab models the proof boundary without real cryptography. prove holds the witness: it checks that the two private addends sum to the public total and that the total stays under the public limit, then emits a ProofArtifact that carries only public data (the total, the limit, and a proof byte length). The witness is consumed here and never travels onward, which is the one rule the lab enforces.

The only change from the starter code is the body of verify, which originally returned false. The verifier takes the Statement and the ProofArtifact and nothing else; its signature does not even mention the Witness type, so by construction it cannot read witness fields. It confirms the artifact's public fields match the statement, that the public total is within the public limit, and that the proof carries non-empty bytes. For the supplied inputs every check holds, so verify returns true.

main then prints the three lines in order. Because the witness (20 and 25) summed to 45 under a limit of 50, prove succeeds with proof_bytes_len = 96; verify returns true; the public total is 45; and the proof byte length is 96, producing exactly the expected output. Crucially, the two values that get printed and could be logged are the public ones, while 20 and 25 never appear at the verification boundary.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should witness generation and verification usually live at different service boundaries?
reviewAnswers.answer: They are different service shapes with different needs: witness generation is heavy, secret-handling compute that belongs on the proving side, while verification is a small, cheap check that only needs the public statement and the proof. Keeping them at different boundaries means the witness never has to reach the verifier, so the secret cannot leak or be over-retained there, and the two lanes can scale and fail independently. Putting both inline in one request handler couples a latency-sensitive edge to expensive proving work and invites storing the witness next to the proof.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes transcript domain separation a protocol rule instead of one local implementation detail?
reviewAnswers.answer: The domain string seeds the transcript and feeds into every challenge the prover and verifier derive, so both sides must use the identical domain to land in the same challenge space. Two different domains are designed to produce different challenges, which is how unrelated protocols avoid sharing challenge space; that is a shared contract between prover and verifier, not a private choice. Changing the domain string during a refactor is therefore a protocol break that makes existing provers and verifiers disagree, even though each component still works locally.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a proof artifact not the same thing as a witness or proving key?
reviewAnswers.answer: The witness is the private input the proof exists to hide, the proving key is a setup artifact the prover needs to produce a proof, and the proof artifact is the public evidence that a valid witness exists for the statement. They have different lifetimes and custody rules: the witness is secret and short-lived and must stay proving-side, the proving key is a large versioned setup artifact, and the proof is versioned transport data that crosses to the verifier. Conflating them is how teams accidentally retain or leak the witness, or treat the proof as if it were as sensitive as the secret it was built from.

reviewAnswers.question: What does zero knowledge fail to protect if public inputs or metadata are already too revealing?
reviewAnswers.answer: Zero knowledge only hides the witness; it says nothing about the public statement, and nothing about side-channel metadata such as proof size, submission timing, or which circuit was used. If the public inputs themselves disclose what the proof was meant to keep secret, the math is still sound but the privacy goal is already defeated. So a proof-backed design can be cryptographically correct and still leak the very information it was supposed to protect through its public surface.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should large proof systems still be reviewed for ordinary Rust concerns such as queues, logging, unsafe wrappers, and resource limits?
reviewAnswers.answer: A proof system has two review surfaces, and sound cryptography still ships an insecure service if the ordinary systems surface is ignored. Queues and resource limits guard against denial of service from oversized artifacts or floods of invalid proofs; logging discipline keeps witness data from leaking at the verifier boundary; and unsafe wrappers around proving libraries carry the same memory-safety risk as any other FFI boundary. Most non-cryptographic failures in these systems come from witness preparation, transcript policy, artifact custody, and integration drift rather than from the prover math, so the boring Rust review is where real incidents are prevented.
